title: Co-founded Microsoft in Albuquerque to sell Altair BASIC
statement: After the January 1975 Popular Electronics cover story on the MITS Altair 8800, Gates and Paul Allen pitched MITS a BASIC interpreter that did not yet exist, wrote it in eight weeks with Monte Davidoff, and on its successful demonstration founded their partnership, registered as Microsoft in New Mexico on November 26, 1976.
outcome: Altair BASIC became the machine's first programming language, the company booked $16,005 of revenue in 1976, and the venture grew into the dominant personal-computer software company, with Gates reviewing every line of code in its first five years.

title: Licensed DOS to IBM while retaining rights to sell MS-DOS to clone makers
statement: When IBM, having failed to license CP/M from Digital Research, asked Microsoft for an operating system, Gates bought a non-exclusive license to Tim Paterson's 86-DOS for $25,000 in December 1980 and full rights for $50,000 more in July 1981, delivering PC DOS to IBM for a one-time $50,000 fee without transferring the copyright.
outcome: Compaq and others cloned the IBM hardware and all needed Microsoft's non-exclusive MS-DOS, which more than ninety percent of American workplace PC users ran by the mid-1980s, converting a small fee into the industry's de facto standard and Microsoft's foundational moat.

title: Shipped Windows 1.0 and rode out Apple's copyright suit
statement: Gates announced Microsoft Windows in November 1983 after seeing Visi On at COMDEX and shipped the first retail version on November 20, 1985, a tiled-window graphical shell over MS-DOS, having secured a license from Apple covering GUI elements used in that first release.
outcome: Reviews were lukewarm, but Windows 3.0 sold 100,000 copies in two weeks in 1990, Gates redirected the company from OS/2 to Windows in 1991, and Apple's 1988 look-and-feel suit largely failed when 179 of its 189 claimed elements were found to be covered by the Windows 1.0 license.

title: Fought the government's antitrust case to settlement instead of breakup
statement: Sued on May 18, 1998 over the bundling of Internet Explorer with Windows, Microsoft saw Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson order the company split in two on June 7, 2000, before the D.C. Circuit overturned the breakup on June 28, 2001, citing the trial judge's misconduct; Gates's evasive videotaped deposition over the meanings of words like compete and we had become a symbol of the defense.
outcome: Microsoft settled with the Justice Department on November 1, 2001, letting PC makers adopt rival software, with obligations expiring in 2007; Gates later called losing the mobile operating system race to Android, during the litigation years, his biggest mistake.

title: Handed the Microsoft CEO role to Steve Ballmer
statement: Gates, who had hired his Harvard friend Steve Ballmer as employee number thirty on June 11, 1980, with a $50,000 salary plus ten percent of profits, made him president in 1998 and chief executive on January 13, 2000, moving himself to chief software architect.
outcome: Ballmer ran the company until February 4, 2014, when Satya Nadella succeeded him; under the transition Microsoft survived the antitrust era and later became the third U.S. public company to pass a trillion-dollar valuation in April 2019.

title: Merged the family foundations into the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation
statement: Having studied Carnegie and Rockefeller philanthropy and started the William H. Gates Foundation with Microsoft stock in 1994, Gates combined three family foundations in 2000 with a five-billion-dollar stock donation to create the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, focused on global health, extreme poverty, and American education.
outcome: The foundation became the world's largest private charitable organization, invested more than $102.3 billion over its first twenty-five years, co-founded Gavi with a $750 million pledge, and helped cut child mortality in half since 2000.

title: Accepted Warren Buffett's $30 billion gift on matching-giving terms
statement: When Warren Buffett pledged roughly ten million Berkshire Hathaway Class B shares, then worth over $30 billion, in June 2006, the foundation accepted conditions requiring Bill or Melinda Gates to stay active in administration and the foundation to give away each year the previous year's Berkshire contribution plus five percent of net assets, doubling its giving rather than swelling its endowment.
outcome: The first 500,000-share tranche was worth about $1.5 billion, Buffett's cumulative giving to the foundation reached roughly $48 billion before the partnership ended in 2026, and the gift funded the expansion into agricultural development, financial services for the poor, and global vaccine programs.

title: Resigned from the Microsoft board to concentrate on philanthropy
statement: In March 2020 Gates left his board seats at Microsoft and Berkshire Hathaway to dedicate himself to climate change, global health and development, and education, after serving as technology adviser to Satya Nadella following his 2014 step-down as chairman.
outcome: The Wall Street Journal reported in May 2021 that the departure came before the board concluded an external law firm's probe, begun in late 2019, into an alleged inappropriate relationship with a Microsoft employee; Gates's philanthropic focus intensified into the 2025 commitment to give away about $200 billion and sunset the foundation by 2045.
